name: Iris Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at an underground zinc mine. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms that drills the holes in the rock face for the explosives. I lead the development crew on my shift, so I check the face, mark up the pattern and make sure nobody gets hurt. We go down the ramp at six, and I'm usually drilling two faces a shift if the ground behaves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when a round pulls clean, every hole doing its job. My dad worked this same mine, and some of the old hands still call me his name. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, because this mine pays less than the big ones and Dev, my fiancé, and I are saving for a wedding in spring. We've got less than a month put away, and most of that is earmarked for the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how it should be. A machine can't feel the ground like a person can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was overblown. At work I'd say let's just keep doing the job well. I don't go online, I'd tell my mum and the ladies at church and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but money's still tight. The wedding, the rent, and Dad's knees mean he can't help out like he used to. That's all still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and take the extra Saturday shifts when they come up. Dev and I would keep the wedding small, sixty people instead of a hundred. And I'd keep everything else the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. A bit tired, thinking about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does cutting the wedding to sixty people mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means some cousins don't come, which my mum won't like. But I won't start married life in debt. My grandmother always said you don't borrow for a party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If something went wrong with the money, who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. Dev's brothers would help, and my uncle has a bit put aside. I'd never go to the government unless there was nothing else.

say: I always thought the AI talk was **overblown**.
At work, I'd say let's just keep **doing the job** well.
I'd only tell my **mum** and the church ladies, not anyone online.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but money is still tight.
The **wedding**, rent and Dad's knees still weigh on us.
do: **Keep drilling** and take extra Saturday shifts.
Cut the **wedding** from a hundred guests to sixty.
Turn to **family** before government if money runs short.
S0.quote: My grandmother always said you don't borrow for a party.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **wedding** and family money, not AI.
She trusts **family** first and avoids government help.
Her identity is tied to her **father's mine**.

steps.text: Take the extra Saturday drilling shifts when offered
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty
Keep rent, food and fuel as they are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. We already have a jumbo upstairs that drills the pattern by itself while the operator watches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and you can't stop progress, but it should be done properly. At work I'd tell the young ones to learn the rock first, the screen second. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't like it. The auto-jumbo upstairs drills the pattern, but it can't tell when the ground's about to fall. Head office doesn't see that, they just see fewer people on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down. I'd cut back on things, maybe postpone the honeymoon. And I'd wait to see whether the auto-jumbo actually works, before I change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry. Like my dad's work doesn't count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if jobs went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in head office who've never been underground. They read reports and think it's all numbers. My dad used to say you can't run a mine from a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What if the auto-jumbo works better than people say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask to be the one who watches it, because I know the ground. But I'm not going to learn computers at home, that's not me. They'd have to train me at work.

say: You can't stop **progress**, but it should be done properly.
Young ones should learn **the rock first**, the screen second.
think: The **auto-jumbo** drills the pattern but can't tell when ground will fall.
**Head office** sees fewer people on the payroll, not the risk.
do: **Keep her head down** and keep drilling.
**Wait** to see whether the auto-jumbo works.
feel: **Uneasy** and angry, as if her father's work doesn't count.
S1.quote: The auto-jumbo upstairs drills the pattern, but it can't tell when the ground's about to fall.
fieldNote: She sees automation as a **head office** decision that ignores ground safety.
She would **only train** if the company trained her at work.
Her **father's** voice shapes her view of the mine.

steps.text: Keep drilling her own faces and stay out of trouble
Postpone the honeymoon to keep the savings
Wait to see if the auto-jumbo upstairs actually works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before our first anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and the church, because the government won't. At work I'd say keep going, there's three years before the robots. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's bad. The planners and the shift bosses go in 2028, then the jumbo drills by itself by 2031. I've never done anything else, and there's nothing else in this town except the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev we put off starting a family until we know where we stand. We'd cut everything, no car upgrade, nothing. I'd ask my uncle about work on his farm in case the mine goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the ground's moving and I can't hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Farm work would also face robots. Would that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, but at least it's family. My uncle wouldn't sack me for a machine. That's the difference between a family and a company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off children. How would Dev take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd understand, but he'd be sad. He wants kids sooner than me. It'd be a hard night.

say: We need to **look after our own**, through family and church.
I'd tell the crew to keep going, because **robots** are three years off.
think: Planners go in **2028**, then the jumbo drills itself by 2031.
I've **never done** anything else, and there's only farming in town.
do: Put off **starting a family** until the future is clearer.
Ask her **uncle** about farm work in case the mine goes.
feel: **Frightened**, like the ground is moving and she can't hear it.
S2.quote: My uncle wouldn't sack me for a machine. That's the difference between a family and a company.
fieldNote: She turns to **family and church** instead of the state.
She expects to **lose her job** by 2031 and has no other skills.
Putting off **children** is the real cost.

steps.text: Put off starting a family with Dev until things settle
Cancel the car upgrade and cut all extras
Ask her uncle about work on his farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two when it comes, thirty-five when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's in God's hands, but we should be sensible. At work I'd keep the crew steady. I'd tell the young ones to get a second trade if they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got a few more years than the fast one, but the end's the same. I'm not going to become a computer person. I'd want to be drilling until the last day they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and save every bit I can after the wedding. We'd still have the wedding, but small. Maybe in a few years I'd look at my uncle's farm properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a slow sad thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell the young ones to get a second trade. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm already the best at this, and I don't want to start again at the bottom. That might be pride. My mum would say it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the mine's going robot and I'd probably be the last of the Patels underground. He'd go quiet. Then he'd say at least I had a good run.

say: It's in **God's hands**, but we should be sensible.
Young ones should get a **second trade** if they can.
think: A **few more years** than the fast picture, but the same end.
I'd want to be **drilling** until the last day they let me.
do: **Keep drilling** and save after the wedding.
Look at her **uncle's farm** properly in a few years.
S3.quote: I'd probably be the last of the Patels underground.
fieldNote: She admits her **pride** stops her retraining.
She expects to **lose the drilling job** in about eight years, when robots arrive.
Family **legacy** is part of her grief.

steps.text: Keep drilling faces for as long as the mine allows
Hold a small wedding in spring with sixty guests
Talk to her uncle about joining his farm in a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then three more for robots. I'd be forty. That's most of a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families and communities should plan. At work I'd say keep going. I'd be less worried than with the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get most of my working life underground. That's what I want. After that, maybe the farm, maybe something else, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling. Dev and I would have kids in a couple of years like we planned. We'd save a bit more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still uneasy about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything to prepare at all, in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a farm course when I'm thirty-five. Something with my hands. Not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your own children about the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard and learn a trade. The mine fed our family for two generations, but it won't feed the third. That's okay.

say: There's time, so **families and communities** should plan.
At work I'd say **keep going**, and I'd be less worried.
think: I'd get most of my **working life** underground, which is what I want.
After that, maybe my uncle's **farm** or something else, God willing.
do: Have **children** with Dev in a couple of years.
S4.quote: The mine fed our family for two generations, but it won't feed the third.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep her **family plans**.
She'd only consider a **hands-on** farm course later, never computers.
Money and a **low-paying mine** still keep her uneasy.

steps.text: Keep drilling faces at the zinc mine
Have children with Dev in a couple of years
Save a little more from each pay every year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, and I've never done anything but drill. What would help is the company training its own people at work, on paid time, and keeping local jobs for local families as long as it can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith and family. People like me don't want handouts. We want to be able to work and look after our own.

headlineQuote: People like me don't want handouts. We want to be able to work and look after our own.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** jumbo drill crew lead at the underground zinc mine her father worked.
She is engaged to **Dev**, saving for a spring wedding with under a month put away.
She is **traditional**, leans on family and church, and won't touch AI.
She grows **alarmed** in the faster pictures, expecting to be the last Patel underground.
With **ten years** she keeps her plans for children and a working life underground.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because she's never done anything but drill.
whatWouldHelp: The company **training its own** people at work on paid time.
Keeping **local jobs** for local families as long as possible.
